title: What to Do With Vested RSUs in India: Sell, Hold, Diversify or Move Them
summary: Should you sell vested RSUs or hold them? A framework for Indian employees: the tax cost of selling now or later, concentration tests and where the money goes.
body_markdown:
Your RSUs have vested, the tax on them has been taken through payroll, and the shares are now sitting in your stock plan account. From here you have four choices: sell them, hold them, sell and diversify into something else, or move them to another broker.


There is no single right answer, but there is a clear way to decide. This guide gives you the tax cost of each choice as an Indian resident, five tests for whether you hold too much of one company, and a way to turn the answer into a rule you can follow at every vest.


It is a framework for making the decision and does not recommend any particular choice. For the tax rules behind it, read[how foreign RSUs are taxed in India](https://paasa.com/blog/how-rsus-are-taxed-in-india) .

## Should I sell my RSUs immediately?


You can, and tax is not a reason to wait. The full value of the shares was taxed as salary on the vesting date, so a sale soon after vesting produces little or no capital gain, and whether you should sell comes down to how much of your wealth already depends on your employer.


The salary tax is due whether you sell or hold. The rupee value taxed at vesting becomes your cost of acquisition, and capital gains tax applies only to the change in value after that date.


If you sell in the same month the shares vest, the cost and the sale value are converted at the same exchange rate (the SBI telegraphic transfer buying rate, or TTBR, on the last day of the previous month). The only gain or loss is the small price movement between the vest and the sale, and you still report it in your return.


Three things can stop an immediate sale, and none of them is a tax rule:


- **A closed trading window:** many listed companies let employees trade only during set windows after results are announced.
- **A lock-up:** shares that vest around an IPO may be locked for a period. Read[RSU lock-up periods explained](https://paasa.com/blog/rsu-lockup-periods-explained) .
- **Settlement:** the shares have to be delivered to your plan account before you can place a sell order.


## Is it better to hold or sell RSUs?


Neither is better by default. Holding a vested RSU is financially the same as receiving a cash bonus and using it to buy your employer's stock, so hold only as much as you would choose to buy today with that cash.


The only difference is that the RSU arrived without a decision, and doing nothing keeps you invested by default.


These are the inputs that should drive the decision:


- **Concentration:** how much of your net worth, including unvested grants, already rides on this one company.
- **Tax:** whether the lot has been held for 24 months or less, or for more than 24 months, and how much gain it carries.
- **Need for the money:** whether you are counting on these shares for a goal in the next few years.
- **Estate tax:** whether your US shares together are worth more than USD 60,000.
- **Conviction:** whether you have a current, specific reason to own the stock beyond the fact that you work there.


Two situations make the decision harder than it should be. If the stock has run up, read[should you sell vested RSUs after a strong stock run](https://paasa.com/blog/should-you-sell-vested-rsus-after-a-stock-run) . If it has fallen below the vest price, read[should you sell vested RSUs if they are in loss](https://paasa.com/blog/should-you-sell-vested-rsus-at-a-loss) .


A weak rupee is not a reason to hold either, because it makes the position look bigger in rupees without making it less concentrated. Read[how rupee weakness changes the way your RSUs look](https://paasa.com/blog/how-rupee-weakness-changes-your-rsus) .


## What waiting for the lower tax rate is worth


Tax is the one input you can put a number on. Foreign shares held for 24 months or less from the vesting date are short-term and the gain is taxed at your slab rate. Shares held for more than 24 months are long-term and the gain is taxed at 12.5% without indexation.


The holding period runs separately for each vesting lot.[Capital gains tax on RSU shares](https://paasa.com/blog/capital-gains-tax-rsu-shares) covers the rules in full.


**Example.** Suppose you are Karan, a product manager in Hyderabad with total income between ₹50 lakh and ₹1 crore. You hold 100 shares of your US-listed employer that vested on 15 April 2025 at an FMV of $200, when SBI's TTBR for 31 March 2025 was ₹85.60 (illustrative). It is now 20 November 2026 and the share trades at $260. Take SBI's TTBR for 31 October 2026 as ₹94.00 (illustrative). You are comparing a sale today with a sale in May 2027, once the lot has been held for more than 24 months, and you assume the price and exchange rate stay the same.


Item Sell now (held 24 months or less) Sell in May 2027 (held more than 24 months)


Sale value (100 × $260 × ₹94.00) ₹24,44,000 ₹24,44,000


Cost of acquisition (100 × $200 × ₹85.60) ₹17,12,000 ₹17,12,000


Capital gain ₹7,32,000 ₹7,32,000


Tax rate on the gain 30% slab rate 12.5%


Income tax ₹2,19,600 ₹91,500


Surcharge at 10% ₹21,960 ₹9,150


Health and education cess at 4% ₹9,662 ₹4,026


**Total tax** **₹2,51,222** **₹1,04,676**


**Left after tax** **₹21,92,778** **₹23,39,324**


### The result: waiting saves ₹1,46,546, which is about 6% of the position


That saving is real, but it is only earned if the share price holds for six more months. If the price falls by more than about 7%, to below roughly $242, Karan is left with less after tax than if he had sold today.


To use this on your own lot, work out what waiting saves as a percentage of its value, then ask whether you would carry the risk of a single stock for that long to earn it.


No tax is deducted in India when you sell, so the tax on the gain is yours to pay as advance tax. Read[advance tax for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/advance-tax-rsu-holders) . For choosing lots, same-day sales and staggered selling, read[how to sell RSUs](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-sell-rsus) .


## How much company stock is too much?


No single percentage works for everyone. A flat limit treats a stable large company the same as a volatile one, and a household with two tech salaries the same as one with income from an unrelated industry.


Size still matters. If 40% of a portfolio is in one stock and that stock falls 30%, the whole portfolio falls 12%, while at a 10% holding the same fall costs 3%. Beyond that, run these five tests on your own position and see how many you fail.


### 1. Would you buy it today?


If the current value of your holding were sitting in cash, would you use it to buy this much of your employer's stock as a fresh investment?


If the answer is no, or "not this much", you are holding the position because it arrived, not because you chose it.


### 2. Does your job fall with the stock?


Ask whether a bad year for the company would also hit your bonus, your job security and your ability to get hired elsewhere in the industry. If it would, your safety net depends on the same company as your shares, and the closer that link, the less of the stock you can afford to hold.


### 3. Have you counted the full position?


Most people count only the vested shares in their account. The real exposure includes unvested units from the original grant and every[refresher grant](https://paasa.com/blog/what-are-rsu-refresher-grants) on top of it.


Unvested units are not yours yet and are usually forfeited if you leave, but they are future wealth you are already planning around. Someone with $80,000 of vested shares, $60,000 still to vest and a new $90,000 refresher is carrying $230,000 of exposure to one company.


### 4. Could you live with half of it gone?


Take the full position from the third test and cut it in half. Would that delay a home purchase, a child's education fund or your ability to get through a gap between jobs?


Falls of that size are not rare for a single company over a few years. If one would derail a near-term goal, the position is too large for that goal, whatever percentage of your net worth it is.


### 5. When do you need the money?


Money meant for a goal many years away can ride out a bad stretch. Money you are counting on in the next one to three years cannot, because there is no time to wait for a recovery.


Liquidity is part of this test. Listed shares can be sold whenever your trading window is open, while shares in a private company cannot be sold until there is an exit.


### Reading your results


You do not need to fail all five. Failing the third or fourth test alone is a reasonable signal to act, and the response is a plan for how much to sell and on what schedule.


## How to build an RSU selling rule


If you decide what to sell on the day the shares land, you are deciding with a price on the screen and no time to check anything. A rule set in advance caps your exposure at a level you chose with a clear head, and it is not a view on where the stock is going.


### 1. Pick one rule type


- **Fixed percentage of every vest:** sell the same share of each vest, anywhere from half to all of it, soon after the vesting date and regardless of price.
- **Cap on the position:** set a maximum share of your portfolio that the stock can represent, and sell enough to get back under it whenever a vest or a rally pushes you over.
- **Time-based drip:** sell a fixed number of shares or a fixed amount every month or quarter, which spreads the exit over time.


Pick one, because the value of a rule comes from having a single thing to check on vest day.


If you are starting with a large position built up over years, you will usually need two parts: a drip or a cap to bring the existing holding down, and a fixed percentage for each new vest so that it does not build up again.


### 2. Run two checks before you sell


**The holding period of each lot.** Every vest is a separate lot with its own vesting date and cost. A fixed percentage rule always sells new lots, so the gain is small. A cap or a drip can reach older lots, where the choice between a lot held for 24 months or less and one held for more than 24 months changes the tax, as in Karan's example.


A lot that is below its vest value produces a capital loss when sold, which can be set off against gains. Read[using capital losses from RSUs](https://paasa.com/blog/using-capital-losses-from-rsus) .


**Your company's trading window.** The dates are set by your employer's insider trading policy and differ from company to company, so check your own policy. Write the window into the rule: sell on vest, or on the first day the window reopens.


### 3. Write it down


Record the percentage or share count, the trigger and the two checks somewhere you will see them. On vest day the stock may be up 20% or down 20%, and both will feel like reasons to wait.


If you want to change the rule, change it on a day when nothing is vesting.


## Where the money goes after you sell


Selling reduces concentration only if the money goes somewhere more diversified, so decide where before you sell.


### 1. UCITS funds vs US-listed ETFs


The usual next step is a broad US-listed ETF. That fixes the single-stock problem but not the estate tax problem.


Shares of US companies and US-domiciled ETFs are US-situs assets. For an Indian resident who is not a US citizen, US-situs assets above USD 60,000 are subject to[US estate tax](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/some-nonresidents-with-us-assets-must-file-estate-tax-returns) at rates of up to 40%. The exemption is given as a credit of USD 13,000, and India has no estate tax treaty with the US.


On US shares worth $500,000, the rate schedule gives a tentative tax of $155,800. After the $13,000 credit, the estate owes $142,800 before your family receives anything.


UCITS funds domiciled in Ireland or Luxembourg can hold the same US companies, but the fund itself is not a US-situs asset. Irish funds bear 15% US withholding on dividends inside the fund, which you cannot claim as a credit in India. Many offer accumulating share classes that reinvest dividends, so no dividend income reaches you to be taxed each year.


Read[UCITS ETFs vs US ETFs for RSU proceeds](https://paasa.com/blog/ucits-vs-us-etfs-for-rsu) for the full comparison, and[how to protect RSUs from US estate tax](https://paasa.com/blog/protect-rsu-from-estate-tax) for the shares you continue to hold.


### 2. Keeping it abroad vs bringing it back


You do not have to bring sale proceeds to India before reinvesting them. Money that is already abroad and is reinvested abroad is not a fresh remittance, so it does not use your USD 250,000 LRS limit and no TCS is collected.


Bringing the money to India is not a taxable event, and you owe the same capital gains tax whether or not the proceeds ever reach an Indian bank account. What the round trip costs is the bank's exchange rate spread on the way in.


If you later send it out again to invest, that is a new LRS remittance with 20% TCS above ₹10 lakh in the year. So the round trip makes sense only for the amount you need in rupees, and the rest can be reinvested from where it is. Read[diversifying RSUs without bringing money back to India](https://paasa.com/blog/diversify-rsus-without-bringing-money-back-to-india) .


### 3. The 180-day rule


Sale proceeds cannot sit as cash abroad indefinitely. Under FEMA, you have 180 days to reinvest them abroad, spend them abroad on a permitted purpose or bring them to India, and the same applies to dividends credited to your account.


Any of the three stops the clock, while moving the cash to another foreign account does not. Read[the FEMA 180-day rule](https://paasa.com/blog/fema-180-day-rule) .


Whatever you buy abroad stays reportable in Schedule FA if you are resident and ordinarily resident.[Schedule FA for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/schedule-fa-rsu-holders) covers the reporting.


## Moving the shares instead of selling them


You do not have to sell to leave your stock plan broker. Vested shares can be transferred in-kind to another broker that accepts Indian residents. Shares in a regular brokerage account usually move by ACATS in 3 to 5 business days, while an employer stock plan account may use the broker's own share transfer process instead, which can take two to three weeks. Selling and wiring the dollars works in every case.


A transfer is not a sale, so it creates no capital gain. Each lot keeps its vesting date and its cost of acquisition, which means the holding period carries on unchanged.


Moving does not reduce concentration or estate tax exposure, because you still own the same US shares. It helps when you want to sell in stages and reinvest from the same account. Read[can I transfer my RSUs to another broker](https://paasa.com/blog/can-i-transfer-my-rsus-to-another-broker) .


## Google RSUs


Everything above applies to Google RSUs. Alphabet is a US company, so its shares are US-situs assets for estate tax and are taxed in India as foreign shares.


The one fact specific to it is the dividend. Alphabet began paying a quarterly cash dividend in 2024 on all of its share classes, and you can check the current amount on[Alphabet's investor relations site](https://abc.xyz/investor/) .


If you hold the shares, the dividend is taxed in India at your slab rate, with credit for the US tax withheld at the 25% treaty rate once your Form W-8BEN is on file. Read[how dividend income from RSU shares is taxed](https://paasa.com/blog/dividend-income-from-rsu-shares-taxed) . Each dividend credited as cash also starts its own 180-day period under FEMA.


Your vesting dates and lot history are in your grant agreement and your stock plan account.


## Meta RSUs


Meta RSUs follow the same rules. Meta Platforms is a US company listed on Nasdaq as META, so the estate tax and capital gains points above apply in full.


Meta also pays a dividend. It began paying a quarterly cash dividend on its Class A and Class B shares in 2024, and each one is announced on[Meta's investor relations site](https://investor.atmeta.com/) .


For a holder in India this means the same as for Alphabet: dividend income to report every year with a foreign tax credit claim, and cash credits that fall under the 180-day rule.


If you work at Microsoft or Amazon, we have separate company guides:[Microsoft RSUs in India](https://paasa.com/blog/microsoft-rsus-india) and[Amazon RSUs in India](https://paasa.com/blog/amazon-rsus-india) .
